keyTakeaways: SurtitleLive uses on-demand runtime delivery so the official viewer avoids loading a full plaintext script bundle up front.
Encrypted subtitle segments are intended to be displayed inside the authorized viewer session, with browser and device behavior still treated realistically.
Temporary access tokens, expiry windows, and server-side revocation controls help limit post-show access.
These controls reduce casual copying and uncontrolled access; they are not a promise of absolute copy protection.

faq.question: How does SurtitleLive reduce casual script copying?
faq.answer: The Official Viewer loads encrypted subtitle segments on demand around the current cue instead of presenting the whole script as one readable browser payload at entry time.

faq.question: Can SurtitleLive guarantee that a script can never be copied?
faq.answer: No digital delivery system can prevent screenshots, cameras, OCR, or custom clients with valid access. SurtitleLive should be treated as risk reduction, not absolute copy protection.

faq.question: What happens if a viewer link needs to be restricted?
faq.answer: Runtime access can be limited through temporary tokens, expiry windows, and server-side revocation for new or renewed runtime requests.

faq.question: How is data protected in transit?
faq.answer: Connections use HTTPS/TLS, and runtime delivery uses encrypted segments as part of a layered security model that also includes access scoping and operational controls.

glossary.definition: A small encrypted subtitle unit requested around show progress rather than a full plaintext script bundle.
The controlled browser session used by an authorized audience viewer.
A server-side control that can limit new or renewed runtime access after a concern is detected.
A security goal that lowers practical copying risk without claiming absolute prevention.
